text: Patent searching is essential for AYUSH innovation: 1) Novelty search — before filing, ensure invention is new. 2) Freedom to operate (FTO) — before commercialization, ensure no infringement. 3) Validity search — find prior art to challenge competitor patents. 4) Landscape analysis — understand technology trends and white spaces. 5) Competitive intelligence — monitor what competitors are filing. Time and money spent on searching saves much more in wasted R&D, failed patent applications, or infringement lawsuits.

Key patent databases for AYUSH: 1) Indian Patent Office (ipindia.gov.in/iponlineservices) — Indian patents and applications. 2) USPTO (patft.uspto.gov, appft.uspto.gov) — US patents and applications, excellent full-text search. 3) Espacenet (worldwide.espacenet.com) — EPO database, covers 100+ countries. 4) WIPO PatentScope (patentscope.wipo.int) — PCT applications. 5) Google Patents (patents.google.com) — user-friendly, good for quick searches. 6) Lens.org — free, powerful, includes scholarly articles. Commercial: Orbit, PatSnap, Derwent Innovation (more features, cost money).

Keyword searching fundamentals: 1) Use synonyms — 'extract', 'fraction', 'isolate', 'preparation'. 2) Use truncation — 'curcum*' catches curcumin, curcuminoids, curcuma. 3) Use Boolean operators — AND, OR, NOT. 4) Search in specific fields — title, abstract, claims, description. 5) Combine botanical names and common names — 'Withania somnifera' OR 'ashwagandha'. 6) Include misspellings — 'ashwaganda' (common error). For AYUSH: also search transliterations of Sanskrit names, vernacular names in different languages.

Patent classifications organize inventions by technology. Key for AYUSH: IPC (International Patent Classification): A61K — Medicinal preparations. A61K 36/00 — Medicinal preparations of undetermined constitution containing material from algae, lichens, fungi or plants. A61K 9/00 — Medicinal preparations characterised by special physical form. A61P — Therapeutic activity. CPC (Cooperative Patent Classification): more granular, used by USPTO and EPO. Strategy: identify relevant classes, browse to find relevant patents, combine with keyword search.

Citation searching leverages patent relationships: 1) Forward citations — who cited this patent? Find newer developments building on prior work. 2) Backward citations — what did this patent cite? Find foundational prior art. 3) Citation networks — map technology evolution. Tools: Google Patents shows citations; Lens.org has good citation features; commercial tools offer advanced citation analysis. For AYUSH: find key patents in your field, trace citation networks to understand technology landscape and identify prior art.

Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL) is essential for AYUSH searches. Content: 2.9 lakh+ formulations from classical texts, translated into patent examiner language (English, French, German, Spanish, Japanese). Access: Patent offices have access; others can request (www.tkdl.res.in). Search: by ingredient, disease, classical text reference. Purpose: primarily for examiners to find prior art, but applicants can check if their invention is documented. For AYUSH: search TKDL before filing to avoid Section 3(p) problems.

Conducting novelty search: 1) Define invention — what's the core novel element? 2) Identify keywords and classifications. 3) Search Indian Patent Office (check if someone beat you in India). 4) Search USPTO, EPO, WIPO for international prior art. 5) Search TKDL for traditional knowledge. 6) Search scientific literature (PubMed, Google Scholar). 7) Review results — focus on claims and examples. 8) Document search strategy and results. 9) Analyze — is invention novel? If prior art found, can claims be narrowed? Do this BEFORE spending on patent filing.

FTO analysis determines if you can commercialize without infringing others' patents: 1) Define your product/process precisely. 2) Identify patents in force in your target markets. 3) Analyze claims of identified patents. 4) Compare your product to each claim element. 5) Assess infringement risk (literal or doctrine of equivalents). 6) Consider design-arounds if high risk. 7) Evaluate patent validity — can problematic patents be invalidated? FTO is crucial before launch; discovery of infringement after commercialization is expensive. For AYUSH: do FTO for key markets (India, US, EU).

Patent landscape analysis provides strategic intelligence: 1) Identify all patents in a technology area. 2) Analyze trends — filing volumes over time, geographic distribution. 3) Map key players — who owns the most patents, who's active recently. 4) Identify white spaces — areas with few patents (opportunities). 5) Cluster technologies — group related patents. 6) Assess patent quality — citation counts, claims scope. For AYUSH: landscape of 'turmeric formulations' or 'ashwagandha patents' reveals competitors and opportunities. Commercial tools help visualize; can also do manually with spreadsheets.

Ongoing patent monitoring: 1) Set up alerts for competitor names as applicant/assignee. 2) Monitor key technology classifications. 3) Track keyword combinations relevant to your R&D. Tools: Google Patents alerts (free), PatentScope alerts, commercial watch services. Frequency: weekly for active technology areas. Action: review new filings, assess impact on your FTO, consider opposition if competitor's patent threatens your business. For AYUSH: monitor key competitors and technology areas relevant to your pipeline.

Scientific literature is prior art: 1) PubMed — biomedical literature. 2) Google Scholar — broad coverage. 3) AYUSH Research Portal (ayushportal.nic.in) — Indian AYUSH research. 4) DHARA (Digital Helpline for Ayurveda Research Articles). 5) Conference proceedings, theses. Publications before patent priority date are prior art. For AYUSH: search for studies on your ingredients/formulations. Your own publications can be prior art — consider timing of publications vs patent filings (file before publishing).

Document your searches: 1) Record search date. 2) Record databases searched. 3) Record search queries used. 4) Save relevant results with notes. 5) Analyze each relevant reference vs your claims. 6) Conclude — is invention novel/non-obvious? Why? This documentation: supports patent application (can cite as prior art searched), defends against inequitable conduct allegations (US), provides basis for strategic decisions, helps patent counsel draft stronger applications. For AYUSH: maintain search records as part of patent file.

When to use professional searchers: 1) High-stakes decisions (major product launch, litigation). 2) Complex technology requiring expertise. 3) Need comprehensive coverage. 4) Don't have time/skills in-house. Types: Patent search firms, Information specialists, Patent attorneys with search services. Cost: Rs 10,000-50,000 for novelty search; more for FTO and landscapes. For AYUSH: professional searchers familiar with TKDL, Ayurvedic texts, and pharma patents add value. Provide clear brief — define invention precisely, specify scope of search.
